title: Park County, CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Park County wells have a 240 ft median depth and 5.5 gpm median yield. Learn what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your property.
h1: Park County water wells: what to expect
intro_html:
Park County wells are classic mountain bedrock wells: most are in fractured granite or similar rock, and depths and yields can swing a lot from one ridge or valley to the next. With over 16,000 wells reporting a total depth and almost 9,500 reporting yield, we have a decent picture of what you’re likely to drill into here.

If you’re looking at land between Fairplay, Hartsel, Jefferson, Como or the more remote parts of the county, the numbers below will give you a realistic range for depth, production, and cost before you call a driller.

sections.heading: How deep Park County wells usually go
sections.html:
Across Park County the median well depth is 240 feet, with the middle half running from 140 to 380 feet. About 48% of wells fall between 100 and 300 feet, and another 32% run 300 to 600 feet, so most drillers will bid assuming something in that range unless geology or nearby logs say otherwise.

Only 12% of wells are under 100 feet, so planning on a very shallow well here is risky. Around 7% go past 600 feet, and the deepest well on record hits 3,500 feet, which shows how unforgiving fractured bedrock can be in the wrong spot. Expect more variability on exposed ridges and better odds of moderate depths in broader valleys.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water is typical here
sections.html:
Park County’s median reported pump yield is 5.5 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 3.0 and 9.0 gpm. That’s generally adequate for a single household on an exempt domestic permit, especially with a decent storage tank.

Most wells do reasonably well: about 57% fall between 5 and 15 gpm and 8% are over 15 gpm. The low end matters, though. About 30% of wells produce 1–5 gpm, which usually works but may require some water management during peak use. Around 5% report under 1 gpm; those can still be workable with storage but are functionally “low-yield” wells and may limit landscaping or future expansion. Always compare a new property to nearby well records, not just county-wide numbers.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend in Park County
sections.html:
Static water levels in Park County have a median of 100 feet below ground, with the middle half between 55 and 160 feet. That means many wells here have 100 feet or more of lift, which affects pump sizing and power use.

Looking at the measurements over time, median static levels were around 40–60 feet from the 1960s through the 2000s. In the 2010s that median dropped to 103 feet, and in the 2020s it sits around 100 feet. That suggests water levels in many parts of the county are deeper now than a few decades ago. It doesn’t mean your well will go dry, but it’s a reason to leave extra pump setting depth and to watch for any local trends if you’re in a heavily built-out area.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and when wells were built
sections.html:
Park County has 22,661 wells in the state records, with 15,366 reported as constructed and 16,108 listing a total depth. Permitting really ramped up starting in the 1970s: about 3,291 permits that decade, 2,854 in the 1980s, and 5,691 in the 1990s. Activity stayed strong with 4,331 permits in the 2000s, then 2,018 in the 2010s and 1,641 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025.

Most wells are for domestic or household use (about 91%), with some stock watering (7%) and a small number of monitoring wells. Drilling is dominated by a few outfits in the records: Allen Drilling & Excavating Co., Inc. (Allen, Jack R.), Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert), and Stan'S Drilling (Stansbury, Larry) show up most often.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Park County
sections.html:
Most Park County wells are drilled in fractured mountain bedrock like granite and gneiss. Typical drilling rates here run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 240-foot median depth, that puts the borehole alone around $15,600–$24,000.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a complete well at that depth usually lands roughly in the $21,600–$36,000 range. Deeper wells in the 300–380 foot “middle half” range scale up from there. When you’re budgeting for a vacant lot outside Fairplay, Hartsel, Jefferson, Alma or Como, it’s smart to assume the higher end of the depth range until you’ve checked nearby well logs and talked to a driller.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: low yield, contamination, and layout
sections.html:
In fractured-bedrock aquifers, the main risk is hitting a tight fracture zone and ending up in that 5% of Park County wells under 1 gpm. There’s also a sizable slice in the 1–5 gpm range, which works for domestic use but doesn’t leave much margin for irrigation or expansion.

On the water-quality side, there are 3 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites, about 31 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles in the county. That doesn’t mean your specific well is impacted, but it’s enough to justify a full lab test on any existing well. Plan your site so the well stays the required separation from septic and future buildings; in shallow valleys and around older subdivisions, well and septic crowding can be an issue.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Park County lot
sections.html:
Before you close on a Park County parcel, pull nearby well records for depth, yield, and static level. With a 140–380 foot middle depth range and a 3.0–9.0 gpm typical yield band, you want to know which side of the curve your specific area tends to fall on.

If you’re buying an existing home, ask for the original well completion report and any recent pump service records, and compare reported static levels to the county-wide medians near 100 feet. For vacant land, assume full well and septic costs in your build budget and confirm that a domestic or household-use permit is allowed. In over-appropriated basins, you may hear about augmentation plans; in most of Park County’s fractured-bedrock areas, individual exempt wells are still the norm, but always verify with the Division of Water Resources.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Park County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across Park County, the median well depth is about 240 feet. The middle half of wells fall between roughly 140 and 380 feet. About 48% of wells are in the 100–300 foot range, 32% are 300–600 feet, and around 7% go deeper than 600 feet. The county’s deepest recorded well reaches 3,500 feet, showing that some locations in fractured bedrock can be much deeper than average.

faq.q: How much water do Park County wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields in Park County have a median of 5.5 gpm, with the middle half of wells between about 3.0 and 9.0 gpm. About 57% of wells produce 5–15 gpm and 8% are above 15 gpm. On the low side, around 30% are in the 1–5 gpm band and about 5% report less than 1 gpm, which are considered low-yield and typically require careful water management and storage.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Park County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Park County’s fractured granite and gneiss, typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 240-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole around $15,600–$24,000. Once you add casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a completed well at that depth usually comes in roughly between $21,600 and $36,000, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Park County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well. Park County has 3 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, about 31 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles, which highlight possible local risks. Many wells provide good-quality water, but you should always test an existing well with a certified lab for bacteria, metals, and other parameters, especially near historic mining or known contamination areas.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Park County wells?
faq.a: Static water level data show median depths around 40–60 feet below ground from the 1960s through the 2000s. In the 2010s the median jumped to about 103 feet, and in the 2020s it’s around 100 feet. That indicates water levels in many wells are deeper now than several decades ago. It’s not a crisis everywhere, but it’s a reason to plan wells with extra pump setting depth and to track local conditions over time.
